title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Vietnam: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Vietnam: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Vietnam: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a Vietnamese citizen living in Viet Nam is planning ahead during a serious or life-limiting illness, putting medical consent designations, notarized mandates, social insurance records, and a compliant will in place while legal capacity remains intact prevents family disputes and court delays. Viet Nam updated several core statutes between 2024 and 2026, including Law on Medical Examination and Treatment No. 15/2023/QH15, Law on Social Insurance No. 41/2024/QH15 (effective 1 July 2025), Law on Notarization No. 46/2024/QH15 (effective 1 July 2025), and Viet Nam's 11 September 2026 entry into the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention. This guide outlines practical planning steps grounded in official Vietnamese sources [1][3][5][7].

steps.title: Palliative care services and health insurance coverage
steps.html:
• Access to clinical palliative care: Under Law on Medical Examination and Treatment No. 15/2023/QH15 published in Government Official Gazette of Viet Nam (Cong bao Chinh phu) and the Ministry of Health national Guidance on Palliative Care (Decision No. 183/QD-BYT), both public and private hospitals provide pain control, symptom management, and interdisciplinary end-of-life care for adults and children [1].
  • Social health insurance (BHYT) and medical records: Verify continuous Health Insurance (BHYT) registration and retain Citizen Identity Card (CCCD), referral papers, and hospital inpatient records so inpatient treatment and home palliative prescriptions qualify for statutory reimbursement via Vietnam Social Security (VSS) [1][4].
  • Care coordination: Confirm pain-medication dispensing protocols and outpatient palliative follow-ups early with the oncology or geriatric hospital department if care will move to the family home [1].

steps.title: Medical consent and designated healthcare representatives
steps.html:
• Statutory patient rights and representative consent: Under Law on Medical Examination and Treatment No. 15/2023/QH15 (effective 1 January 2024), patients hold statutory rights to information about diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment refusal, and may name or designate a representative to give medical consent if capacity is later lost [1].
  • Recording treatment wishes clearly: Because Viet Nam has no separate standalone statutory living-will act independent of medical-law consent rules, record your family member's resuscitation, hospitalization, and comfort-care wishes directly in the hospital chart alongside signed family contact designations while capacity is intact [1][2].
  • Avoid informal instructions: Written notes kept only at home carry less clinical weight in emergency wards than signed chart directives linked to the named medical representative [1].

steps.title: Notarized authorizations, banking mandates, and guardianship
steps.html:
• Powers of attorney and notarization rules: Under Civil Code No. 91/2015/QH13 and Law on Notarization No. 46/2024/QH15 (effective 1 July 2025, recognizing both in-person and regulated electronic/online notarization with mandatory verification safeguards), your family member can execute a Power of Attorney (Giay uy quyen) or Authorization Contract (Hop dong uy quyen) for banking, pension collection, and administrative filings [2][3].
  • Capacity and termination limits: Under Civil Code agency principles, an ordinary authorization terminates when the grantor loses civil act capacity or dies, so set up co-authorized bill-payment mandates early and prepare medical evidence if court-supervised guardianship under the Civil Code becomes necessary [2].
  • Property and banking check: Confirm with local banks whether branch-specific internal bank signature forms are required in addition to a notarized Hop dong uy quyen [2][3].

steps.title: Social insurance, disability, and retirement benefits
steps.html:
• Law on Social Insurance No. 41/2024/QH15: Administered by Vietnam Social Security (VSS) and published on Government Portal of Viet Nam (Civil Status and Social Insurance Laws), the 2024 law (effective 1 July 2025) replaced the base salary benchmark with the statutory reference level (muc tham chieu) and reduced the minimum contribution period for an old-age pension from 20 years to 15 years [4][5].
  • Sickness, disability, and early retirement assessments: Review eligibility for prolonged sickness allowance, medical-assessment early retirement upon reduced working capacity, and voluntary vs. compulsory social insurance balances through the VssID digital portal and Vietnam Social Security (VSS) offices [4][5].
  • Employment leave documentation: Working caregivers should review Labor Code leave allowances and maintain hospital treatment certificates to support workplace medical or family-care arrangements [4][5].

steps.title: Wills, civil status records, and 2026 Apostille preparation
steps.html:
• Executing a notarized or commune-certified will: Under Part Four of Civil Code No. 91/2015/QH13 and Law on Notarization No. 46/2024/QH15, signing a will before a notary office or Commune-level People's Committee reduces post-death probate disputes; confirm compliance with mandatory reserved shares for qualifying minor or incapacitated heirs [2][3][6].
  • Organizing civil and property files: Gather Citizen Identity Card (CCCD), birth and marriage extracts governed by Law on Civil Status No. 60/2014/QH13, land-use right certificates (Red Books), and insurance beneficiary records [6].
  • Apostille vs. Article 12 consular legalization: Since 11 September 2026 (Decree No. 293/2026/ND-CP), public documents used abroad may obtain an Apostille through Consular Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Viet Nam (MOFA) or Ho Chi Minh City Department of Foreign Affairs, except for documents destined for Germany, Austria, or Czechia, which filed Article 12(2) objections and still require consular legalization [7][8][9][10].
